source: George, Walker & Monster (2019) Does strategic planning improve organizational performance? A meta-analysis, Public Administration Review 79(6)
finding: Random-effects meta-analysis of strategic planning and organisational performance. The pooled link is positive and small to moderate. Heterogeneity is very high. This is generic strategic planning, not scenario planning.
numbers: 87 correlations from 31 studies: r=.229, 95% CI [.186,.271], I2=91.6%, tau2=.032. One effect per study (31): r=.255, CI [.177,.333], I2=91.3%. Authors call it small to moderate, closer to moderate. A Wikipedia summary gave 'about 9,000 organisations'; that figure was not found in the paper text read here.
limits: Correlational primary studies, mostly survey self-report. Strategic planning is not scenario planning; scenario use is not a moderator. Corrects b07: the effect size is now known.
agent_relevance: A plan-like scaffold may carry a modest benefit on average, but the spread across studies is huge, so one average does not justify adding a step.

source: George, Walker & Monster (2019) meta-regression and publication bias
finding: Formal and comprehensive planning did not differ; participatory planning had a weaker effect. Studies using several data sources found smaller effects (common-source bias). Publication-bias tests disagreed.
numbers: Meta-regression explains about 71% of effect-size variance. Constant .417 (SE .108) when performance is effectiveness, planning is formal, data are single-source. Public vs private and US vs non-US: no significant difference. Begg test z=1.88 (n.s.); Egger bias coefficient 2.651, p<.001. Authors say publication bias cannot be neglected.
limits: Moderator model clustered on 31 studies with many dummies. Effects shrink when the data source is independent of the survey.
agent_relevance: Effects are largest when the rater is the one who did the planning. Score scenario benefit with an outside grader, not self-report.

source: Rohrbeck & Kum (2018) Corporate foresight and its impact on firm performance: a longitudinal analysis, Technol Forecast Soc Change 129:105-116
finding: Longitudinal firm study. Foresight maturity vs need ('future preparedness') was measured in 2008. Performance came from S&P Capital IQ in 2015, relative to industry peers. Foresight here is a broad capability, not scenario planning alone.
numbers: 467 firms invited, 135 responded (29%), 52 dropped for incomplete or inconsistent data, 83 kept. Profitability data for 70 firms; market-capitalisation data for 42 listed firms. Questionnaire: 35 maturity items, 10 need items. Only 36% of firms were 'vigilant' (adequate foresight); 62% were at or below maturity level two; 2% reached level four.
limits: Observational, self-selected sample, self-rated maturity, no control. Differences judged by a 15% descriptive threshold, not significance tests. Secondary sources gave 70 or 83 firms; both are right for different steps.
agent_relevance: Best longitudinal firm study found, but not causal.

finding: Vigilant firms were over-represented among 2015 outperformers. The cross-sectional 2008 link was reversed, so the time lag matters. Case notes on moves by vigilant firms add qualitative support.
numbers: Vigilant share: 63% of outperformers vs 24% of underperformers. No 'neurotic' or 'in danger' firms among profit outperformers. Migration: of vigilant firms 40% moved up a profitability cluster, 55% held, 5% (1 firm) fell; only 9% of deficient firms moved up. Profitability 16% vs industry 12% (33% more than average); deficient firms 37-44% lower profitability. Market-cap growth 75% for vigilant firms vs 25% sample average (authors: '200% additional growth'); deficient firms' discount -49% to -108%. In 2008 cross-section, outperformers were on average LESS prepared than underperformers.
limits: Small subsamples (70 and 42). The reversed cross-section suggests good performers under-invest in foresight. Reverse causality and survivorship not ruled out. No confidence intervals.
agent_relevance: Shows only that foresight capability correlates with later industry-relative performance. No mechanism tested, so it cannot justify a scenario operator by itself.

source: Schoenegger, Jones, Tetlock & Mellers (2025) Prompt Engineering Large Language Models' Forecasting Capabilities, arXiv 2506.01578
finding: Preregistered Study 1 tested 38 prompts, including 'Hypothetical Scenario Analysis' (imagine scenarios where the event does or does not occur) and 'Premortem' (success and failure chains), against a control prompt. Scenario prompts gave no reliable Brier gain. Closest direct test of a scenario step vs a no-scenario arm for calibration.
numbers: 100 binary ForecastBench questions, 4 models (mean Brier: Claude 3.5 Sonnet 0.208, Haiku 0.214, GPT-4o 0.215, Llama 3.1 405B 0.227). Difference vs control for Hypothetical Scenario Analysis: -0.007 Brier (lower is better), p=.411, Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p=.774. Premortem -0.008, adjusted .774. In a simpler one-sample table scenario analysis was -0.012, p=.027 uncorrected; after correction only Frequency-Based Reasoning, Base Rate First and Step-Back beat control, and Bayesian Reasoning and Propose-Evaluate-Select were worse.
limits: Single-turn prompt, not a multi-step scenario operator. Token budget not matched (longer prompts). Effects tiny vs noise (Brier SD about 0.16).
agent_relevance: Answers gap 1 in part: a one-prompt scenario step does not beat control on calibration. Base-rate prompts did better. Put the base rate before any scenario step.

source: Schoenegger et al. (2025) Study 2: compound prompts and reasoning models
finding: Combining Hypothetical Scenario Analysis with Premortem or Step-Back did nothing. Only a superforecaster-written Conditional Odds-Ratio prompt moved accuracy, and it made forecasts worse.
numbers: Same 100 questions, 6 models including o1 (Brier 0.216) and o1-mini (0.217); Sonnet 0.207, GPT-4o 0.208, Llama 0.218. Step-Back + Hypothetical Scenario: -0.001, adjusted p=.985. Hypothetical Scenario + Premortem: +0.004, adjusted p=.985. Mean forecasts 41.5% to 44.8%. About 19,000 forecasts targeted per model; 1,674 to 1,893 returned for three models (refusals).
limits: Refusals reduced returned forecasts. A null result does not show scenarios hurt, only that this wording did not help.
agent_relevance: Justify a scenario step by other outcomes (option quality, risk list), not by forecast accuracy.

source: Secondary summary of 'Can Language Models Use Forecasting Strategies?' (search result page)
finding: Reported: the most basic LLM prompt beat a human prediction-market baseline, and no more complex strategy (base rates, arguments for and against) improved on it.
limits: Seen only through a search snippet. Primary paper not opened. Not independent evidence until read.
agent_relevance: Consistent with d05: extra reasoning scaffolds rarely add forecast accuracy.

source: Kanis, Mann & Stumpf-Wollersheim (2026) AI-augmented strategic decision-making under time constraints, Strategy Science 11(1):75-92
finding: Probably the '348 participant' experiment in gap 3. It is a startup-evaluation task, not scenario planning. LLM use widened breadth, cut depth and reduced consensus of mental representations. It neither improved nor harmed foresight accuracy.
numbers: N=348; 2 (time pressure) x 2 (LLM use) between-participants. No effect sizes obtained. Publisher page returned 403; only a search abstract and a synopsis page were seen. Synopsis also notes more information overload.
limits: Not opened in full. Foresight accuracy is startup-outcome judgement, not scenario quality. Do not cite numbers.
agent_relevance: Warns that a breadth-adding step (like a scenario fan) can add breadth without accuracy. Pair it with a convergence step.

source: Meissner & Wulf (2013) Cognitive benefits of scenario planning: its impact on biases and decision quality, Technol Forecast Soc Change 80(4):801-814
finding: Controlled experiment. The bias tested is framing bias, not anchoring (earlier notes assumed anchoring). Scenario planning reduced framing bias and raised decision quality more than traditional strategic planning tools.
numbers: 252 graduate management students. Abstract page read only; cell sizes and effect sizes unavailable (paywall). A secondary note says a complete scenario process seems needed for the debiasing.
limits: Student sample, one decision case. Full text not read, so no numbers beyond N.
agent_relevance: Best controlled human test of scenarios against another tool. Suggests a framing check: restate the decision in gain and loss frames.

source: Spaniol & Rowland (2023) AI-assisted scenario generation for strategic planning, Futures & Foresight Science
finding: A reflections-from-practice article, not an experiment. It argues AI can generate many scenarios at almost no cost, but usefulness depends on the user's skill in drawing out raw material. AI supplies base material and is unlikely to replace human practitioners.
numbers: No measurements. Authors Spaniol (Roskilde) and Rowland (Penn State Altoona).
limits: Opinion piece. Closes the 'Spaniol and Rowland numbers' question: there are none. Read via Crossref abstract summary.
agent_relevance: Cost is not the limit; selecting and using scenarios is.

source: Kozachek (2026) Entering the age of hybrid futures: human vs GPT-generated scenarios, Futures 176
finding: Only metadata retrieved (sole author, Futures vol 176, Feb 2026). Abstract and numbers could not be obtained.
limits: Not opened. Gap 8 stays open for this paper.

source: The Time Machine: Future scenario generation through generative AI tools, Future Internet 17(1):48 (2025)
finding: Search snippet: a GPT-4-based tool tested in six trials with 222 participants. GenAI scenarios sparked discussion in most cases with good prompting; authors say critical human use stays essential.
numbers: 6 trials, 222 participants (snippet). No outcome scores retrieved.
limits: Page returned 403. Snippet only. Participant-rated usefulness; no control arm known.
agent_relevance: Quality depended on prompt quality, in line with d10.

source: Klein & Linneman (1983, 1984) multiple scenarios in US industrials; environmental assessment international study (search snippets)
finding: Survey work from the Diffenbach era. About 150 of the Fortune 1000 industrials used multiple scenario analysis in formal planning, and firms did not follow the rigorous procedures the literature recommends.
numbers: About 150 of the Fortune 1000 (snippet). No satisfaction rates retrieved.
limits: Emerald page returned 403. Snippet only; wording may be imprecise.
agent_relevance: Adoption was real but procedure was loose, which fits the de Geus point that execution varies.

source: Diffenbach (1983) Corporate environmental analysis in large US corporations, Long Range Planning 16(3):107-116 (catalogue record)
finding: A catalogue record confirms the paper exists (Long Range Planning, June 1983, subject 'Business planning -- Surveys'). Its findings on scenarios, including 68%, could not be checked in any source opened here.
numbers: 68% of large firms and 'third most popular technique' remain known only through Wikipedia.
limits: Gap 5 stays open for Diffenbach: original text not obtained; no satisfaction data found. Author name not shown in the record.

source: Phelps, Chan & Kapsalis (2001) Does scenario planning affect performance? Two exploratory studies, J Business Research 51(3)
finding: Secondary reviews say scenario use went with better financial performance but possibly worse customer service. Descriptions of the sample disagree (two firms in one review; British water companies and IT consultancies in a blog), so the design is not verified.
limits: Not opened (ResearchGate and ScienceDirect blocked). Exploratory, tiny sample, correlational. Gap 4 stays open for Phelps.
agent_relevance: Do not cite as causal evidence.

source: Wulf, Meissner & Stubner (2010) A scenario-based approach to strategic planning, HHL Working Paper 6
finding: Conceptual paper with one consulting case (German photovoltaic industry), no experiment. It says scenario processes are hard to replicate, vary a lot, rely on unstructured workshops, and experts rarely disclose methods. It proposes a structured process with a Framing Checklist and a core strategy plus options from scenarios.
quote: many scenario experts are reluctant to completely disclose their methodologies
limits: Case illustration only. Useful for process shape, not effect.
agent_relevance: Supports an explicit, repeatable scenario operator with stated steps rather than free narration.

source: Murphy (2026) Agentic forecasting with structured linguistic beliefs (BLF), arXiv 2604.18576
finding: A search agent with a structured belief state (probability plus evidence summary) topped compared agents on ForecastBench. No scenario step appears in the text searched.
numbers: 400 historical ForecastBench question-date instances; highest overall Brier Index among compared external agents; only method to significantly beat a crowd+empirical-prior baseline. Full text searched: no mention of 'scenario'.
limits: Backtest, not live. Scenario operator absent, so silent on gap 1.
agent_relevance: Updating a written belief with evidence has a measured gain; scenario narration has not.

source: Gap check: de Geus follow-through and implementation-rate data (gap 7)
finding: No source found in this pass that measures implementation rate with and without scenarios. No numeric version of the de Geus audit exists in the pages reached.
limits: Absence in a limited search (8 searches; several publishers blocked; APIs rate-limited). Not proof none exists.
agent_relevance: Treat follow-through as a design principle, untested.

source: Gap check: number of scenarios and actor-name bias with a scaffold (gaps 6 and 9)
finding: No experiment found that varies the number of scenarios against decision quality. No study found where a scaffold removes the CFPD actor-name bias. c06 shows the bias exists; d05 shows prompt tweaks rarely move accuracy.
limits: arXiv, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar APIs were rate-limited in this run, so coverage is thin.
agent_relevance: Label actors neutrally and test the effect in our own bench; do not assume a scaffold fixes it.
